name: Darwin
title: Thickness Gauging Darwin: Livestock Carriers, LNG & Supply Ships
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Darwin for livestock carriers, LNG carriers, tankers and offshore supply vessels: decks, ballast tanks, holds and piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement in Darwin Harbour and at East Arm
intro: Darwin is Australia's northern door to Asia. Livestock carriers load cattle for Indonesia and Vietnam at East Arm Wharf, LNG carriers lift cargoes from the gas plants on the harbour's shores, and tankers, container ships and offshore supply vessels work alongside. A ship lift at East Arm is due to start staged operations in 2027; until then, most gauging here happens at the berth or at anchor. For each job our technicians fly from India to Darwin and join the ship.

highlights.h: Livestock carriers on a short Asian run
highlights.p: Cattle ships make frequent voyages between Darwin and Southeast Asian ports, and many are conversions of older ships. Effluent and wash-down water attack livestock deck plating, drains and the structure below, so regular gauging between voyages keeps owners ahead of the problem.

highlights.h: A ship lift coming to East Arm
highlights.p: The Northern Territory government is building the Darwin Ship Lift Facility at East Arm as part of the Northern Marine Complex, for defence, commercial and offshore vessels. Once staged operations begin in 2027, docking-period gauging will be possible in Darwin itself.

highlights.h: Big tides, heat and the wet season
highlights.p: Darwin Harbour has a large tidal range and strong streams, and the wet season from November to April brings heat, humidity, storms and cyclone risk. Tank entry plans allow for heat stress, and anchorage boardings are timed to the tide.

port.h: Darwin Harbour: livestock, gas and the gateway to Asia
p: Darwin Harbour is a large drowned river valley opening onto the Beagle Gulf and the Timor Sea, with deep water and several arms running inland. The commercial port is at East Arm Wharf, on the south-eastern side, where container, general cargo, bulk, livestock and fuel ships berth together with offshore supply vessels. Fort Hill Wharf, close to the city centre, takes cruise ships and visiting naval vessels. The gas plants occupy their own sites on the harbour: INPEX's Ichthys LNG plant at Bladin Point and the Darwin LNG plant at Wickham Point, each with its own loading jetty. Tides are large by Australian standards and drive strong streams through the harbour, so berthing, pilotage and small-boat transfers are planned around them. Ships waiting for a berth anchor where the port directs, inside or outside the harbour.

Livestock is Darwin's signature trade. Cattle from Northern Territory stations, along with stock trucked from neighbouring states, are loaded onto livestock carriers for Indonesia, Vietnam and other Asian markets, with the busiest months in the dry season. Container ships and general cargo ships connect the Territory with Asia and the rest of Australia, product tankers bring in fuel for the north, and bulk carriers load mineral exports. LNG carriers serve the two gas plants. Offshore gas fields in the Timor Sea and beyond are supported from Darwin, so supply and support vessels are regular callers, and the harbour is also home to fishing and pearling fleets, border protection craft and naval units. Cruise ships arrive in the dry season, when the weather is settled and the tropical heat eases a little.

For ship inspection, Darwin's geography is what matters. For many ships arriving from Asia it is the first Australian port, and for many leaving it is the last call before a Southeast Asian yard. That makes it a useful place to collect readings on a ship heading for docking, and a place where owners want confidence in the condition of ships trading on the short Asian runs. The livestock fleet deserves particular attention: these ships work hard in heat and humidity, many were converted from older car carriers, container ships or general cargo ships, and their structural condition is checked by charterers, insurers and AMSA. The ship lift at East Arm will change the local picture by giving smaller commercial, offshore and defence vessels a docking option in northern Australia.

facilities.h: East Arm Wharf, the anchorage and the new ship lift
p: Today Darwin has no dry dock for deep-sea ships, so gauging is done alongside or at anchor. East Arm Wharf is the main place to work: a livestock carrier between voyages, a tanker discharging fuel, a container ship on its regular call or a supply vessel back from the fields can each give access to some combination of decks, ballast tanks, holds and piping. Livestock carriers are best gauged before the cattle arrive or after the decks have been washed out, because loading days are crowded and the decks are in use. At the anchorage, a ship waiting for a berth can be boarded by launch, with transfers timed to slack water where possible.

The Darwin Ship Lift Facility, part of the Northern Marine Complex at East Arm, is under construction for the Northern Territory government. Marine piling began in 2026, and staged operations are planned from 2027, serving defence, commercial and international vessels. Until it opens, docking for larger ships means a Southeast Asian yard, and smaller local craft use the harbour's existing slipways. The LNG jetties at Bladin Point and Wickham Point are controlled terminals where electronic equipment and deck work are restricted, so gas carrier gauging is normally kept to permitted locations or planned for elsewhere.
list: East Arm Wharf: livestock carriers, tankers, container and general cargo ships; deck, ballast tank and hold gauging during the stay
Supply vessel berths at East Arm: tank, deck and seawater piping gauging on offshore supply vessels between campaigns
Harbour anchorages: owner's condition and pre-purchase gauging by launch, timed to the tide
Fort Hill Wharf: deck and accessible tank readings on visiting ships near the city centre
Ichthys and Darwin LNG jetties: limited deck and piping readings on gas carriers where the terminal allows
Darwin Ship Lift Facility (staged operations from 2027): docking-period gauging on smaller commercial and offshore vessels

context.h: AMSA, livestock carrier rules and northern biosecurity
p: AMSA carries out port state control in Darwin within the Tokyo MoU and Indian Ocean MoU frameworks that cover all Australian ports. Livestock carriers receive particular attention: AMSA certifies ships for the carriage of livestock under Marine Order 43 and inspects them in Australian ports, looking at structure, ventilation, drainage, fodder and water systems and the ship's general condition. A livestock carrier with wasted deck plating, corroded pen supports or failing drainage can lose its certificate or face a detention, and in a trade built around short, frequent voyages that means lost business quickly. Owners who keep a current thickness record on livestock decks and the structure supporting them are better placed to answer questions from AMSA, from charterers and from the exporters who book the ships.

Darwin's position facing Asia makes biosecurity a live issue. International arrivals must report their biofouling management through the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry's Maritime Arrivals Reporting System, and ballast water is managed under the department's requirements; the city's marinas have dealt with an introduced mussel incursion in the past, which is part of why northern Australia takes marine pests seriously. The tropical climate is the other factor. High temperatures and humidity speed up coating breakdown in ballast tanks and void spaces and drive condensation corrosion under decks, so ships in long Asian and northern Australian service tend to show wastage sooner than their age suggests. In the wet season, heat stress also limits how long a technician can safely work in an enclosed tank, which affects how a job is scheduled.

jobs.h: Typical thickness measurement jobs in Darwin
jobs.p: Darwin jobs revolve around the livestock fleet, the ships heading to Asian yards and the offshore support fleet. For livestock carriers, owners usually want deck and ballast tank condition between voyages, either to plan repairs or to support a sale. For ships leaving for a docking, the job is a pre-docking estimate that turns into a steel figure for the yard specification. Offshore supply vessels between campaigns give longer jobs with full tank access, and tankers discharging fuel allow deck and piping checks. Once the ship lift opens, docking-period gauging on smaller vessels will join the list. We plan the scope with the superintendent, arrange access through the agent, and travel from India once dates are confirmed; reports follow the class TM formats.
list: Condition gauging of livestock decks, pen supports and double-bottom tanks on a cattle carrier between voyages from East Arm
Pre-docking steel estimate on a bulk carrier loading mineral exports before it sails for a Southeast Asian yard
On-hire gauging of an offshore supply vessel's tanks, deck and seawater piping before a Timor Sea campaign
Pre-purchase gauging of a converted livestock carrier at the harbour anchorage
Deck and cargo pipe wall-thickness readings on a product tanker discharging fuel at East Arm

logistics: The team flies into Darwin International Airport, which has international links to Asia and domestic connections through other Australian cities; East Arm is a short drive from the city. Indian technicians need an Australian visa covering short-term specialist work, which is arranged before departure. The ship's agent arranges port and berth access, and visiting technicians work under the escort arrangements the port and terminals set. Wet-season storms can disrupt flights, so travel in that period is planned with some slack.

faqs.q: Can a livestock carrier be gauged during a Darwin loading?
faqs.a: Only in a limited way. On loading day the decks are full of cattle and stock handlers, and the master's priority is a safe, quick load. Ballast tanks that are empty and tested can sometimes be gauged, but livestock decks and their supports are best measured before the cattle arrive or after the ship has been washed down between voyages. We plan with the owner to catch that gap.

faqs.q: When will the Darwin ship lift be able to take a vessel?
faqs.a: The Northern Territory government's published plan is a staged start to operations in 2027, after defence qualification of the facility. Dates for commercial dockings will depend on how operations are rolled out. When it opens, smaller commercial and offshore vessels will be able to dock in Darwin, and we can gauge them on the lift or on hardstand. Larger ships will still dock in Asia.

faqs.q: Do Darwin's tides affect work at the anchorage?
faqs.a: Yes. The harbour's large tidal range produces strong streams, and launch transfers are easier and safer around slack water. We plan anchorage boardings with the agent and the launch operator to fit the tide table, and allow for the possibility that a transfer is postponed. Work alongside at East Arm is less affected, although gangway arrangements change as the tide rises and falls.

faqs.q: Is the wet season a problem for tank gauging in Darwin?
faqs.a: It makes the work harder rather than impossible. Between November and April, heat and humidity inside ballast tanks and voids can be severe, so entries are shorter, ventilation is essential and the team rotates to manage heat stress. Cyclones can also close the port for a time. Where a choice exists, a wider scope is easier to complete in the dry season.
